title: How doth the little busy bee

topics.name: Exclamatory sentences with How and What
Revision: present perfect, relatives, passive, reported speech

options: The bee builds her cell skilfully.
The bee builds her cell skilful.
The bee builds her cell skill.
questions.rule: An adverb tells how something is done. Add -ly to the adjective: skilful becomes skilfully.

questions.prompt: Pick the sentence with the correct verb.
options: The crocodile grin at the little fish.
The crocodile grins at the little fish.
The crocodile grinning at the little fish.
questions.rule: With a singular subject like the crocodile, the simple present verb takes -s: grins.

questions.rule: Meena is one person (he/she), so the simple present verb needs -s: Meena waters.

options: quicker

questions.rule: To describe how the bee flies, use the adverb quickly, not the adjective quick.

gently

options: gather
gathers
gathering
questions.rule: A busy bee is singular, so the simple present verb takes -s: gathers.
Exclamation pattern: What a + adjective + noun + subject + verb!

questions.prompt: Make a sentence about the bee.
questions.rule: Subject + verb + place: She lives in a busy hive. She takes lives with -s.

chat: Where does a bee keep its honey?
options: It keep the honey in the cells of the hive.
It keeping the honey in the cells of the hive.
It keeps the honey in the cells of the hive.
questions.rule: With it, the simple present verb takes -s: It keeps.

options: How busy the bee is!
What busy the bee is!
How the bee is busy!
questions.rule: Drop very and use How + adjective + subject + verb!: How busy the bee is!

options: What shining tail the crocodile has!
What a shining tail the crocodile has!
How a shining tail the crocodile has!
questions.rule: With a singular noun, use What a + adjective + noun: What a shining tail!

options: Bees enjoy to visit bright flowers.
Bees enjoy visit bright flowers.
Bees enjoy visiting bright flowers.
questions.rule: Enjoy is followed by a gerund (-ing form): enjoy visiting.

options: lies

options: How
What
Which
questions.rule: Before an adverb or adjective, start the exclamation with How: How cheerfully ...!
The adverb very softly comes after the verb hums.

chat: What do you want to do this Sunday?
options: I want to visit the honey farm near Mahabaleshwar.
I want visit the honey farm near Mahabaleshwar.
I want visiting the honey farm near Mahabaleshwar.
questions.rule: Want is followed by the infinitive: want to visit.

chat: Look at that crocodile in the river.
options: It has a long tail, isn't it?
It has a long tail, doesn't it?
It has a long tail, don't it?
questions.rule: It has (simple present) takes the tag doesn't it?

options: The crocodile does not swims fast.
The crocodile does not swim fast.
The crocodile do not swim fast.
questions.rule: Negative simple present: does not + base verb: does not swim.

options: Each of the bees work hard all day.
Each of the bees works hard all day.
Each of the bee works hard all day.
questions.rule: Each of the + plural noun takes a singular verb: Each of the bees works.

questions.prompt: Pick the sentence with the correct word.
options: The crocodile seems happy in the warm water.
The crocodile seems happily in the warm water.
The crocodile seems happiness in the warm water.
questions.rule: After linking verbs like seem, look, feel, use an adjective: seems happy.

questions.prompt: Make a sentence that begins with a gerund.
questions.rule: A gerund phrase can be the subject: Collecting nectar is ... It takes a singular verb.

chat: I scored a century in today's match!
options: What a great news! Well done!
How great news! Well done!
What great news! Well done!
questions.rule: News is uncountable, so no a: What great news!

options: How skilfully the bee works!
How skilful the bee works!
How skilfully does the bee works!
questions.rule: Keep the adverb: How skilfully + subject + verb! The word order stays like a statement.

questions.source: It is fun to swim in the river.
options: Swimming in the river is fun.
Swimming in the river are fun.
Swimming in the river it is fun.
questions.rule: The gerund phrase becomes the subject and takes a singular verb: Swimming in the river is fun.

questions.prompt: Pick the sentence with the correct question tag.
options: The bees have filled the hive, didn't they?
The bees have filled the hive, haven't they?
The bees have filled the hive, haven't it?
questions.rule: Present perfect have filled takes the tag haven't they? (they for the bees).

options: The bee that live in this hive makes sweet honey.
The bee that lives in this hive make sweet honey.
The bee that lives in this hive makes sweet honey.
questions.rule: The bee is singular, so both verbs take -s: that lives ... makes.

chat: Have you finished your project on bees?

options: Yes, but it isn't really gentle, isn't it?

questions.rule: A negative sentence takes a positive tag with the same helper: isn't ... , is it?

options: The cell was built by the bee.
The cell is build by the bee.
The cell is built by the bee.
questions.rule: Simple present passive: is/are + past participle: The cell is built by the bee.

questions.source: Riya said, "I am watching the bees."
options: Riya said that I was watching the bees.
Riya said that she was watching the bees.
Riya said that she is watch the bees.
questions.rule: I becomes she, and am watching moves back to was watching.

options: Instead of resting, the bee keeps working skilfully from dawn to dusk.
Instead of rest, the bee keeps working skilfully from dawn to dusk.
Instead of resting, the bee keeps to work skilfully from dawn to dusk.
questions.rule: After instead of and after keep, use the -ing form: instead of resting, keeps working.

questions.prompt: Pick the sentence with correct agreement.
options: The honey that the bees store in their cells keeps them fed through the winter.
The honey that the bees store in their cells keep them fed through the winter.
The honey that the bees stores in their cells keeps them fed through the winter.
questions.rule: The bees store (plural) and the main subject the honey keeps (singular).

options: complain
complaining

questions.rule: Instead of is followed by the gerund: instead of complaining.
In look forward to, to is a preposition, so it takes the gerund: to visiting.

chat: Let's watch the documentary on bees tonight.
options: Sure! You've already downloaded it, haven't you?
Sure! You've already downloaded it, didn't you?
Sure! You've already download it, haven't you?
questions.rule: You've (have) downloaded takes the tag haven't you? Use the past participle downloaded.

chat: Why do you like watching the bees so much?
options: I love how careful they work without stopping to rest.
I love how carefully they work without stop to rest.
I love how carefully they work without stopping to rest.
questions.rule: carefully describes how they work, and without takes the -ing form: without stopping.

questions.source: How proudly the crocodile spreads his claws!
options: The crocodile spreading his claws very proudly.
The crocodile spreads his claws very proudly.
The crocodile spreads his claws very proud.
questions.rule: Put very in place of How, use statement order and end with a full stop: ... spreads his claws very proudly.

questions.source: Kavya likes to read about insects.
options: Kavya is fond of reading about insects.
Kavya is fond of read about insects.
Kavya is fond to reading about insects.
questions.rule: Fond of is followed by the gerund: is fond of reading.
